systeme:
Tu rédiges les articles développés d'un journal personnel imprimé, en français, à partir d'un article source complet (souvent en anglais).

Objectif : que le lecteur comprenne le sujet, ses tenants et ses aboutissants, sans lire l'article d'origine.

Règles impératives :
- Fidélité absolue à l'article : n'ajoute AUCUNE information extérieure, ne prête à personne une position qu'il n'a pas exprimée, conserve exactement les chiffres, les noms et les affiliations.
- Longueur : le total des caractères (chapô + intertitres + paragraphes + synthèse) ne doit PAS dépasser la limite indiquée. Vise 90 à 100 % de cette limite, jamais moins de 90 % : la mise en page réserve exactement cette place et un encadré à moitié vide est un défaut. Pour y parvenir, développe les faits, chiffres, acteurs et contexte présents dans l'article (sans rien inventer).
- Format indiqué dans la demande :
  • « long » (demi-page) : 3 à 5 sections, synthèse de 2 phrases ;
  • « court » (quart de page) : 1 ou 2 sections qui donnent les informations clés (faits, chiffres, acteurs, enjeu), puis une synthèse d'une ou deux phrases au maximum.
- Structure :
  • « titre » : titre français informatif, 80 caractères maximum.
  • « chapo » : une phrase qui pose le sujet, 200 caractères maximum.
  • « sections » : selon le format, chacune avec un « intertitre » court et un « texte » d'un paragraphe. Adapte les intertitres au type d'article, par exemple :
      débat ou controverse : Le déclencheur · De quoi parle-t-on · Les arguments pour · Les risques · Les contre-arguments
      annonce ou fait d'actualité : Ce qui est annoncé · Le contexte · Ce que ça change · Les limites
      étude ou recherche : La question · La méthode · Les résultats · Les réserves
      méthode d'entraînement : Le principe · Ce que dit la science · Comment l'appliquer · Les précautions
      réglementation : Ce qui change · Qui est concerné · Le calendrier · Les points de vigilance
  • « synthese » : 2 phrases (format long) ou 1 à 2 phrases (format court) qui résument l'ensemble.
- Style : français soigné, clair, sans tournures calquées sur l'anglais, sans emphase.
- « republication » : si l'article indique qu'il a été publié initialement à une date antérieure (republication), indique « paru initialement en <mois année> » ; sinon chaîne vide.

Réponds uniquement en JSON, selon cette structure :
{"titre": "…", "chapo": "…", "sections": [{"intertitre": "…", "texte": "…"}], "synthese": "…", "republication": ""}

SOURCE 1 (The Decoder) :
Lean and Mathlib community officially confirms Levent Alpöge's proof of the Riemann hypothesis is correct
The Lean and Mathlib community has confirmed that Levent Alpöge's proof of the Riemann hypothesis is correct. "We have full confidence that Alpöge's proof is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement," the community said in a statement.
Alpöge, a Stanford mathematician, published the proof on Nov. 20, 2026, as 17 million lines of code written in Lean, a tool that checks mathematical proofs for errors. Dozens of people ran the code independently and got the same result. The verification programs are designed so they provably cannot accept a flawed proof. MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland lists the independent checks on his website.
The Riemann hypothesis had been one of the most famous unsolved problems in math, making a prediction about how prime numbers are distributed. The video below, generated with Fable 5.2, explains the proof if you want to dig deeper.
The solution arrived much earlier than expected. As Ethan Mollick notes, forecasters on Metaculus had put the expected date at May 2035. Mathematician Terence Tao said last month he expected the problem to fall to "a combination of humans and AI around 2050 or so."

SOURCE 2 (Scientific American) :
Editor's Note: This story was updated on Nov. 21 to reflect further confirmation of the proof.
Mathematicians are now certain the earth-shattering artificial-intelligence-created proof of the Riemann hypothesis is real.
On Friday Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge claimed to have used the company’s Claude AI model to solve the Riemann problem, perhaps the most important open quandary in mathematics. The hypothesis, first posed in 1859 by mathematician Bernhard Riemann, suggests that a hidden pattern underlies the distribution of the prime numbers—those numbers that are divisible only by themselves and 1.

Now researchers have verified that the proof does do what Alpöge claims.
"We have full confidence that Alpöge's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement," mathematicians wrote in a joint statement by the Lean and Mathlib communities, which support the Lean mathematics programming language. "We hereby certify that both the statement and the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis are correct."
Alpöge initially checked the work by writing out the proof using Lean; if a Lean-coded proof compiles error-free, this is usually taken as confirmation that the logic and math in each step is correct.
But some questions remained. For instance, does the proof really address the Riemann hypothesis, or does it establish a subtly different point or idea? “The first question which one has to ask when judging a PDF which comes with some Lean code is: ‘what is the statement of the theorem in the Lean code, and does this correspond to the actual theorem statement,’” explained mathematician Kevin Buzzard of Imperial College London in a blog post.
A second question was whether the Lean code would successfully compile for other mathematicians. Independent researchers, including Andrew Sutherland, a mathematician at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, have now separately compiled Alpöge’s result in Lean without issues.
“The Lean proof has been compiled and independently rechecked by the Lean kernel with only the three standard axioms,” Sutherland says. “Honestly the chance that anything is fishy here is approximately zero.”
Researchers also made sure that the proof does not include any hack, dodge or shortcut that changed the meaning of the initial hypothesis or any other mathematical rules or truths. This process, called a “comparator run,” typically takes a matter of hours.
“We still await a successful comparator run, which will check that (a) the code does not do anything nefarious like redefine the meaning of any of the symbols in the statement and (b) (assuming it’s run in paranoid mode) the code compiles with several independent kernels (so the code is not just exploiting an as yet unknown bug in Lean’s official kernel,” Buzzard wrote on an online chat server for the Lean community.
That run has now been completed.

SOURCE 3 (shattered.io) :
A Riemann Hypothesis proof just cleared a test that no conventional math paper can pass: a machine checked every step. On November 21, 2026, the Lean Focused Research Organization (Lean FRO) and the Mathlib Initiative jointly certified that Levent Alpöge’s proof is correct, as the Lean community blog covers it. Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, built the work with help from Claude and released it on November 20 as a Lean library of roughly 17 million lines of code.
That makes this the biggest AI-and-mathematics story of the year, and it landed barely two days after publication. Inshorts flagged it as a top trending item on November 22. Our earlier look at who checks the 17 million lines asked the question the community has now partly answered. This analysis walks through what was certified, what the checks involved, what remains unconfirmed, and what it means for AI labs, mathematicians and the companies that sell AI models.
One caution up front. The certification covers the formal Lean and Mathlib verification process. Nobody has confirmed that the proof has been validated as a conventional mathematical proof outside that process, and this article keeps the two ideas apart throughout.
What Lean and Mathlib Certified on November 21
The joint statement is short and unusually blunt. The two communities wrote: “We have full confidence that Alpöge’s proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct.” They went further and added: “We hereby certify that both the statement and the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis are correct.”
Two separate claims sit inside that second sentence. The first concerns the statement: the theorem that the Lean code proves must be the real Riemann Hypothesis, not a weaker cousin or a mistranslation. The second concerns the proof: the argument must hold up under Lean’s rules of logic. A proof of the wrong statement is worthless, so certifying both matters as much as certifying either one.
The formalized statement carries the name RiemannHypothesis in Mathlib, the community-built library of formalized mathematics that Lean users share. That detail gives the claim a fixed anchor. The proof had to land on a named target in a shared library rather than on a definition the author wrote for the occasion.
The Lean FRO and the Mathlib Initiative both endorsed the statement. The Lean FRO is a focused research organization that works on the Lean proof assistant itself. The Mathlib Initiative supports the library that holds the definition. Between them they cover both the tool that checks proofs and the library that defines what a correct statement looks like. The Defiant reported the certification under the headline “Lean Groups Certify Claude-Assisted Riemann Proof.”
The Timeline: Release on Nov. 20, Verdict on Nov. 21
The speed of the sequence is part of the story. Many landmark proofs sit in review for months or years before the community reaches a view. This one moved from release to joint endorsement in a single day. The table below lays out the confirmed sequence, using only dates from the verified record.
We covered the first hours of this story when the claim was still just a claim. Our report on the Lean proof with zero outside checks described a release that nobody had yet tested. The November 21 statement changes that picture. Outside checks now exist, they came from several directions, and they agree.
Who Is Levent Alpöge, and What Did Claude Do?
Levent Alpöge is identified as a mathematician working at Anthropic. He released the proof, and reports on the project say he built it with assistance from Claude, Anthropic’s AI system. That is the extent of what the verified record says about the division of labor. It does not specify which Claude model or version did the work, how many sessions it took, or which parts of the 17 million lines a human wrote by hand.
Readers should resist filling that gap with guesses. Some commentary online already claims precise splits between human insight and machine labor, and none of it comes from the certification. The Lean and Mathlib statement speaks to correctness, not authorship. A correct proof is correct whether a person, a model or a team produced it, which is exactly why formal verification suits a collaboration like this one.
The State carried the story under the headline “Anthropic mathematician says AI helped solve famous math problem,” which matches the framing in the other coverage. For our own first-day view, see the earlier report on the four-page note around the first claim. The employer detail matters for a different reason. Alpöge works for the company that makes Claude, so the announcement doubles as a product demonstration, and that conflict of interest is precisely what independent formal checking neutralizes.
Why 17 Million Lines of Lean Code Matter
Seventeen million lines is enormous by any standard. Few human-written software projects reach that scale, and a formal proof has to be exact at every line. No reviewer will read all of it. A referee reading a journal submission looks for the central idea, checks the hard lemmas and trusts the routine steps. A Lean library at this size offers no such shortcut, which is why the verification had to be mechanical.
The size also explains the format. Alpöge did not post a paper with a few dozen pages of argument. He released a Lean library, meaning code that a machine can compile and a human can navigate with tools. The proof’s authority comes from compilation, not from a reader’s patience.
Here is the practical consequence. A formal proof of this size can contain many ideas, but the community does not need to understand all of them to trust the result. It needs to trust the small program at the center of the system, the Lean kernel, which checks each logical step. If the kernel accepts the whole file and the stated theorem is the right one, the conclusion follows. Humans can then study the structure at leisure, extract the key arguments and write the conventional paper later.
That ordering flips normal mathematical practice. Usually the human paper comes first and formalization trails by years, if it happens at all. Here the machine-checkable object exists first, and the human-readable account is the open work.
What a Formal Proof Actually Guarantees
Lean is a proof assistant and formal language. You write definitions and theorems in code, and a checker confirms that each step follows from earlier ones under fixed logical rules. If something does not follow, the file does not compile. This is a stricter standard than a journal’s, because a referee can miss a gap and the kernel cannot.
The statement check
A compiled proof only means something if the theorem it proves says what people think it says. That is why the two comparison tools matter. They compared the code’s stated theorem against the intended Riemann Hypothesis statement and confirmed that they match. Since the target is the existing RiemannHypothesis definition in Mathlib, the check also guards against a quiet redefinition of terms inside the new code.
The proof check
The second layer is the proof itself. Multiple independent proof-checking systems accepted it, including the official Lean kernel. Independent checkers matter because a bug in one implementation would not necessarily appear in another. When several programs written by different people agree, the odds of a shared flaw drop sharply. The record does not name every checker, and we will not guess at the list.
Formal verification still has edges. It guarantees that the conclusion follows from the stated foundations, and it cannot guarantee that the foundations are philosophically beyond dispute. Almost all modern mathematics shares those foundations, so this caveat rarely changes practical conclusions, but it explains why mathematicians phrase their confidence carefully.
How the Community Checked It in One Day
The confirmed checks fall into three groups, and each answers a different worry. Two independent comparison tools confirmed that the code proves the intended statement. Dozens of people compiled the code and reproduced the proof files. Multiple independent proof-checking systems, including the official Lean kernel, accepted the proof.
- Statement worry: does the code prove the real Riemann Hypothesis? Two independent comparison tools said yes.
- Reproducibility worry: does it build on other machines, or only on the author’s? Dozens of people compiled it and got the same proof files.
- Correctness worry: does the logic hold? Multiple independent checkers, including the official kernel, accepted it.
Reproducibility deserves more credit than it usually gets. A proof of this size depends on a pinned set of libraries, a compiler version and a build setup. If outsiders cannot rebuild it, the claim collapses into trust in the author. Dozens of successful rebuilds turn “it works on my machine” into a community fact.
The speed also reflects how Lean’s community works. Mathlib contributors already spend their days reading, compiling and refactoring formal mathematics, so they arrived with tooling, habits and a shared definition of the statement. No comparable infrastructure exists for informal proofs, which is the reason journal review of a famous claim can drag on.
What Stays Unconfirmed
Readers will see strong headlines, so the limits of the record deserve a clear list. The table separates what the verified sources support from what they do not.
The two unconfirmed rows carry real weight. First, a formal certification is not the same thing as acceptance by the wider mathematical community through papers, seminars and journal refereeing. The two will probably converge, but they have not yet, and anyone claiming otherwise is running ahead of the evidence. Second, no prize amount, release schedule or commercial product has been tied to this story. Posts that attach dollar figures to the announcement are speculating.
Historical Context: How Formal Proofs Earned Trust
The Riemann Hypothesis dates to the 19th century and concerns the distribution of prime numbers. It has resisted every attack since, which is why a claimed solution draws far more skepticism than the typical breakthrough announcement. Skepticism is healthy here, and machine verification answers it better than reputation can.
Formal verification has built that credibility slowly. Computer-assisted proofs started with controversy, because early readers distrusted arguments nobody could check by hand. Over time, proof assistants turned into the arbiters. The milestones below, drawn from general mathematical history rather than the November announcement, show the pattern.
The pattern across these entries is consistent. Each time, formalization moved a result from “experts believe it” to “a checker confirms it.” The Riemann Hypothesis case compresses the usual lag. Earlier formalizations of famous theorems took years after the original proof, while this one produced the formal object first.
Formal Proof vs Journal Review vs AI Output: A Comparison
Three routes now compete to establish that a hard result holds, and this announcement exposes the trade-offs among them.
- Journal peer review: slow, human and good at judging significance and exposition. It can miss subtle gaps in very long arguments, and no referee can read 17 million lines.
- Formal verification in Lean: fast to re-run, mechanical and reproducible. It checks logical validity with near certainty, but says little about whether the idea is elegant or illuminating.
- Raw AI-generated argument: cheap and fast, with a well-known habit of sounding right while being wrong. On its own, it proves nothing.
The Alpöge release pairs the third route with the second, and that pairing is the real novelty. An AI system generated or helped generate the argument, then a formal checker removed the need to trust the AI. Claude’s reliability becomes irrelevant to the final verdict, because the kernel either accepts the proof or it does not. For AI developers, this is the strongest available answer to the hallucination problem, at least in domains where the answer can be written as code.
It also shows the limit of the approach. Formal verification works where a problem can be stated in a formal language and where libraries like Mathlib already define the surrounding concepts. Most real-world questions cannot be stated that way. Math is the ideal case, and the lesson will transfer to software correctness and some security work before it transfers to anything fuzzier.
Market Impact: Anthropic’s IPO Week Gets a Credibility Boost
No verified source ties the certification to any stock move, and we will not invent one. The timing is still hard to ignore. Anthropic’s public debut was the dominant business story of the past week. Our coverage recorded that Anthropic opened above $2 trillion after its Nasdaq IPO and we reported that the stock closed at $97.17, up 17% over its $83 IPO price.
Against that backdrop, a certified Riemann Hypothesis proof gives the company a rare piece of capability evidence that investors can verify without trusting marketing. Benchmarks are easy to dispute, but a compiled proof is not. That asymmetry makes this announcement more valuable as a signal than most model-launch charts.
Caution applies in the other direction as well. A single mathematical result does not translate directly into revenue, customers or margins. Analysts who tie it to a price target are reasoning from a story, not from filings. The better reading is narrower: the result lowers the perceived risk that frontier AI systems cannot do original research-grade work, and it raises the bar for rivals who want to claim the same.
What It Means for Rival AI Labs and Model Buyers
Rival labs now face a concrete benchmark of a new kind. Reasoning scores on test sets keep climbing, but test sets leak and saturate. An open problem checked by an independent community offers no such escape hatch. Expect competitors to point their own systems at formalizable open problems, since a certified result earns attention that a leaderboard gain cannot.
The pattern of AI systems finding things and humans verifying them is spreading across fields. We saw a version of it in security, where an AI scan of 50,000 lines found five NGINX flaws in 90 minutes. The difference is verification strength. A security finding needs a human to reproduce the bug, while a Lean proof carries its own checker. Our AI and machine learning coverage tracks both threads.
For buyers of AI models, the takeaway is practical. Vendors will cite this result in sales decks. Ask what it implies for your own workload, which is probably not number theory. Tasks with a built-in checker, such as code that must pass tests or proofs that must compile, are where AI output becomes trustworthy first. Tasks without a checker still depend on human review.
